name: PT Fore Kopi Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Fore Kopi: a store machine the cash flow does not yet pay for
frontmatter.summary: Fore Kopi is Indonesia's fastest-growing listed coffee chain: about ninety net new outlets in 2025, revenue up by more than half again in the first nine months of 2026, and an operating margin that widened as the central cost base was absorbed. We initiate at SELL with a target of Rp286. Once the rent on every outlet is charged, the base case sits at a fraction of the price and the multiple cross-check is lower still.
thesis: Unit growth is the engine and it is executing: the estate reached 322 outlets at the end of 2025 from a much smaller base a year earlier, another 100 are planned for 2026, and nine-month revenue of 1,597 IDR bn is already ahead of the whole of the prior year [S2][S3][S4].

The operating leverage is real, not forecast: the cost ratio fell as stores were added because the central kitchen, head office and technology base were built ahead of the estate, and the nine-month operating margin of 5.7% is struck after rent and after the owned-asset depreciation charge [S4].

The lease is the part of the model the market is not paying for: rent of 150 IDR bn in FY2025 and 152 IDR bn in nine months of 2026 is a financing outflow, so free cash after rent and capex is negative and the growth is being funded from the IPO proceeds, not from operations [S2][S4].

The valuation argument is about duration, not the near term: the price implies revenue growth of 39.0% against our 26.0% in every forecast year, so the market is paying for a store programme that outgrows ours for a decade and for a mature margin above today's [S2].

The multiple cross-check is struck on trailing earnings and therefore understates a business growing at this rate; the de-rating risk in a premium-multiple consumer name with a 21.1% float is the strongest case against us [S0][S4].

catalysts.event: FY2026 results: the first full-year read on whether the store programme held the operating margin, on capex against the company's own budget, and on cash after lease payments
First-quarter 2027 trading: store openings and revenue per outlet once the strong nine-month base of 2026 is in the comparator
Annual general meeting and public expose: FY2027 store target, capex budget, the funding plan for the rollout and any change to the no-dividend policy
Year-end store count against the planned additions, and the first trading read on the Fore Donut format and the central kitchen
Any decision on the Singapore footprint and on the free float, which the controlling shareholder could address through a secondary sale

blocks.text: **SELL — target Rp286, total return -48.4% against a Rp555 share price.**

Fore Kopi sells coffee through company-operated outlets under the Fore brand, and it has done the difficult part of a retail roll-out: it has opened stores quickly without losing the gross margin that pays for them. The estate reached 322 outlets at the end of 2025, almost all coffee shops in Indonesia with a handful in Singapore, and the company plans another 100 this year [S2][S3]. Revenue has followed the store count almost mechanically: Rp1,497.1bn in FY2025 against Rp1,038.7bn the year before, and 1,597 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 alone [S2][S4].

The operating story is better than the top line. Because the central kitchen, head office and technology base were built ahead of the estate, each additional store has dropped through to profit: operating income reached 131 IDR bn on a gross margin of 61.7%, and net profit attributable to shareholders was 90.0 IDR bn, up by about half [S4]. Depreciation is charged in full inside those figures: the pack carries Rp187.7bn, which the notes decompose into owned depreciation of 88.2 IDR bn plus right-of-use depreciation of 105 IDR bn, the pack's line being the part charged outside cost of sales [S2].

The correction is why this is not an initiation on a premium multiple. The corporate FCFF adds back depreciation, including that of the leased estate, and subtracts capex, but never subtracts the rent that pays for the leases, because Indonesian filers report lease payments inside financing. Uncorrected, the model values Fore on a cash flow no landlord would accept: on FY2025 figures, operating cash flow of 317 IDR bn less capex of 192 IDR bn less lease payments of 150 IDR bn was negative before any growth spending [S2]. We charge the rent inside the free cash flow instead: operating cost carries the lease payments on every outlet the forecast implies, only owned depreciation is added back, and the 30 September lease liability comes out of net debt because the obligation is served in the cash flow [S2][S4]. The DCF is then worth Rp195 a share and the base value Rp166, against a price of Rp555.

The target is that base case rolled forward one year at the cost of equity, Rp185, weighted with the mirrored scenarios at Rp286: the bull at Rp743 is what a faster estate is worth after it pays its own rent, and the bear at Rp33 is worth more than a static deduction showed because a smaller estate owes less rent [S4]. The point of the rating is that it does not depend on the tail: the base case alone is worth a fraction of the price, and the cross-check on trailing earnings is lower still.

What today's price needs is a demanding set of assumptions: a mature margin above the one the model reaches, or a discount rate below the one the sovereign and the company's beta imply. At the peer median of 9.6 the shares are worth Rp97, and the market pays 48.6x of this year's earnings and 35.4x of next year's. The reverse DCF says the price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 39.0% against our 26.0%, and because the solver moves the whole growth path, the market is asking for a store programme that outgrows ours in every forecast year, not for one good quarter [S2].

The cash position is the second reason for caution, and it is not in the base case's story. Cash fell from Rp327.5bn at the 2025 year-end to 233 IDR bn at the end of September 2026, as capex of 191 IDR bn plus lease payments of 152 IDR bn outran operating cash flow of 280 IDR bn, and the company raised no new equity or debt to fill the gap [S4]. The FY2026 capex budget of 250 IDR bn is company-stated and the rollout is company-led, so the programme is credible; but it is funded by running down the IPO proceeds. FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is Rp-24.6bn, negative because rent and the store build outrun the EBITDA they generate, so a funding event is a risk to the base case's growth as well as the bear case's outcome, and the discounted placement into a float of 21.1% is the bear mechanism [S0][S4].

Two things move the value beyond the rent: gross margin, which the annual contracts and price locks protect in 2026 and reset in 2027 [S3], and store productivity, where revenue per average outlet is the only honest read on cannibalisation because the company discloses no same-store sales, and it has risen only modestly [S2][S4]. Everything else — the tax rate normalising, the negative working capital, the absence of a dividend — is second order against those two and the lease.

Fore Kopi is a Jakarta-based food and beverage company that operates coffee shops under the Fore brand, with roasted coffee as its core product and an "affordable premium" positioning: premium product and packaging, a comfortable and deliberately photogenic store format, and a price point below the international chains [S2]. It was founded in 2018, opened its first outlet in Senopati in Jakarta, launched its own ordering application in the same year, and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in April 2025 after an initial public offering of new shares that represented 21.1% of the post-offering capital [S2].

The estate is company-operated rather than franchised. Outlets are grouped into flagship, medium and satellite formats by size and design, and the company runs them directly, which keeps the customer experience and the margin under its own control but puts the fit-out cost and the lease on its own balance sheet [S2]. At the end of 2025 the group operated 322 outlets. All but a handful are coffee shops in Indonesia, a small number are in Singapore following the Bugis Junction opening in 2023, and the remainder are the new Fore Donut format launched during 2025 [S2]. Domestically the network covers Greater Jakarta and other cities in Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Bali, so the expansion is no longer a single-city story [S2].

The revenue mix is a coffee story with a food attachment. Beverages produced roughly nine tenths of FY2025 revenue, food about a tenth, and other income a rounding error, with beverages grown in-store from espresso-based preparation and food supplied through the central kitchen and pastry/donut lines [S2]. The nine-month figures show the same shape: net revenue of 1,597 IDR bn is struck after a discount line large enough to tell you how much of the top line is promotional rather than list-price demand, with beverages still the overwhelming majority and food a materially smaller contributor [S4]. The donut format is the company's attempt to lift food attachment and basket size without adding another coffee format; it is small enough today that its success or failure changes the mix rather than the level of revenue [S2][S3].

The channel is omnichannel in a literal sense. Offline sales run through the company-operated outlets; online sales run through the Fore Coffee application and through third-party delivery platforms including Gojek, Grab and ShopeeFood [S2]. Management treats the own-app channel as a strategic asset for customer data and loyalty rather than only as a sales channel, and the annual report discloses reliance on third-party booking platforms as a named risk, with commission decisions and application outages cited as the exposure [S2].

Strategy for the next phase is explicitly about quality of growth rather than store count alone. Management describes selective expansion based on location analysis and organisational readiness, a stronger food contribution, better outlet productivity and data-driven decisions, with the 2026 capital budget split between the coffee format, the donut format and a central kitchen [S2][S3].

The group is controlled by Fore Holdings Pte. Ltd., a Singapore holding company that the annual report identifies as the controlling shareholder and that holds no other operating assets; the register shows the controlling holder at 78.9%, a token residual with PT Otten Coffee Indonesia, and the public holding the remainder of a float of 21.1% [S2][S0]. We use the company's register rather than the data pack's insider figure, which is larger and does not reconcile with the float [S2]. The controlling shareholder's board representatives are tied to East Ventures, the venture investor that seeded the business, and the president commissioner is an East Ventures founder [S2]. Fore is therefore venture-backed rather than a family conglomerate: fast decision-making and a controlling holder with a long horizon, but a thin independent check and a float that stays small until the sponsor sells down.

On market position the company is a challenger, not the leader. It does not publish a market-share number and says explicitly that it will not use an unpublished estimate to claim one, describing its position instead as strengthening with the store count [S2]. We take that at face value: the estate is large enough to be a national format and far too small to set category pricing, which is exactly the position from which a challenger either compounds or gets squeezed [S2].

Fore competes in the chained coffee segment of Indonesian foodservice. The reference point the company uses is a Redseer study cited in its prospectus, which puts the Indonesian Foodservice Roast Coffee category at 5.5 USD bn and places chained coffee inside it as a subcategory still on a growth trajectory [S2]. We treat that number as an order of magnitude rather than a forecast, and so does the company: the annual report says explicitly that the projections should be read as an indicator of market direction, not as realised market size, and that it will not use an unpublished estimate to claim share [S2]. That is unusually candid and it sets the evidentiary bar for this section: the category is large and growing, but nobody in the public record knows exactly how large or how fast.

The demand drivers are behavioural and they favour the format. Out-of-home coffee consumption has been rising, a majority of surveyed consumers drink coffee outside the home at least weekly, and the stated reasons are socialising with friends and family, trying better and more varied coffee, and enjoying the outlet atmosphere rather than simple convenience [S2]. Retail food and beverage sales and digital payment transactions grew strongly through 2025, with QRIS transactions growing at a triple-digit rate, which matters because the coffee ticket is small, frequent and increasingly cashless [S2]. The same disclosure also names the counter-driver plainly: rising global coffee prices put a premium on supply discipline, pricing and cost efficiency, and seasonal factors swing volumes [S2].

Geographically the market is still an urban Java market with an outer-island tail. Greater Jakarta accounted for about half of the chained coffee market in the Redseer study, Java outside Jakarta for roughly three tenths and the rest of the country for the remaining fifth, which is why every national chain, Fore included, is trying to convert outer-island presence from a flag-planting exercise into a profitable density story [S2]. That structure cuts both ways for a challenger: the core market is where the competition and the rents are, and the periphery is where the growth is but also where the logistics and the unit economics are hardest.

Our own driver decks barely touch this name, and that is a feature. The agricultural and soft-commodity deck prices palm oil, soyoil, wheat, corn and soymeal; green coffee, dairy and packaging are not in it, and the only route to Fore's P&L is through pastry and donut inputs, so we set both cost links to zero and describe the exposure here [S3]. The channel that does matter is the currency: imported beans, dairy and packaging are priced off the dollar, so a weaker rupiah raises input costs with a lag, and management's response has been price locks and annual contracts [S3]. Macro demand matters more than macro cost: real incomes, fuel prices and purchasing power drive the frequency of a small discretionary ticket, and fuel-price pressure is already flagged for 2026 [S3].

Competition is intense and the company says so. The annual report describes a crowded market in which consumers choose on comfort, spatial experience, menu variety and the social function of the outlet, not on the product alone, and in which raw-material and seasonal pressure decides who survives [S2]. The five forces point the same way: buyer power is high because switching cost is close to zero, supplier power is moderate because coffee and dairy are globally priced, substitutes are plentiful across tea, ready-to-drink and other out-of-home occasions, new entrants keep coming because a single outlet is cheap to open, and rivalry is high because the large chains are all opening stores at once [S2]. The barrier that actually binds is site quality and the central infrastructure behind it, which is where an incumbent estate of 322 outlets has an advantage over a new entrant [S2].

Regulation is light on the product and heavy on the accounting. There is no price control on coffee and no licensing regime comparable to the extractive sectors; the relevant rules are the lease standard that puts store obligations on the balance sheet, disclosure rules for a listed company, and the exchange's free-float requirement, which the current float satisfies [S2][S0]. The practical consequence is that the reported numbers are sensitive to lease accounting: the lease liability and the right-of-use asset move with the store programme, and the financing cash flow carries rent payments that never appear in operating cash flow [S2][S4].

Our moat verdict is narrow. Brand, store density and the own application are real assets, and gross margin holding while the estate grew by about two fifths suggests some pricing power at the shelf [S2]. But the company discloses no same-store sales, the category has no switching cost and the competition is well funded, so we do not underwrite a widening moat: the valuation fades returns toward the cost of capital rather than assuming current economics persist [S2].

Chained coffee is a category where the second-order economics decide the winner. The first store is
a marketing expense; the hundredth is a logistics problem; the thousandth is a property company
with a coffee habit. Between those stages the fixed cost of the central kitchen, the training
organisation and the ordering platform has to be carried by a store base that is still growing,
which is why so many chains show rapid revenue growth and disappointing profit. The tell is whether
the operating cost ratio falls as stores are added, and whether the stores being added are close
enough to the existing ones to share the cost of serving them.

The record is short but it is internally consistent. Revenue went from Rp286.7bn in FY2022 to Rp1,497.1bn in FY2025, EBITDA from Rp17.7bn to Rp293.3bn, and net profit attributable to shareholders from a loss to Rp90.1bn [S2]. The company was barely profitable in FY2023, its first positive year after rebuilding the estate through the pandemic, so the current margin is not a cyclical peak inherited from a benign base; it is the first period in which the store base, the central kitchen and the overhead have been sized to each other [S2]. That matters for the forecast: we are not extrapolating a boom, we are extrapolating the first normal year.

The revenue build is store-led and the arithmetic is public. Nine-month net sales of 1,597 IDR bn are already above the whole of FY2025 and grew by more than half on the prior year, with the store count the dominant driver and revenue per average outlet rising only modestly [S4][S2]. Management guided to top-line growth of about 50.0% and net profit growth of about 70.0% for 2026 [S3]. We take the revenue guide and not the profit guide, and the reason is the tax line rather than the operating line: nine-month profit grew about half, not 70.0%, because the effective tax rate normalised to roughly the statutory rate in 2026 against almost nil a year earlier, when accumulated losses shielded profit and the nine-month charge was a small fraction of pre-tax income [S4]. Our FY2026E rate of 26.0% lets the fourth quarter come in slightly below the nine-month rate as the deferred tax asset is used [S4]. On the operating line the nine months support the company: operating income rose from 131 IDR bn against a prior-year figure less than half as large, and the second half of the year carries the new stores opened in the first [S4]. FY2026E growth of 50.0% therefore reconciles to both the guide and the actual: a fourth quarter at a slower rate than the first nine months still gets the year to Rp2,245.7bn. We then fade to 26.0% in FY2027E and to 20.0% the year after, because the incremental store adds a smaller percentage to a larger base and because the company itself frames 2026 as selective rather than accelerated expansion [S3]. The long-run rate is 5.0%, below nominal GDP, which is the right assumption for a leased estate that matures to replacement capex.

Margins are the part of the story that the market underrates, but the reported ratios need a bridge to the model. Gross margin has been stable at 61.7% in FY2025 and essentially the same in the nine months of 2026, despite coffee and dairy inflation, because the mix of beverages and food has been margin-neutral and the company locked input prices [S2][S4]. Operating expenses were Rp818.6bn in FY2025, a little over half of sales, carrying right-of-use depreciation but not the lease payments, which Indonesian filers put in financing; the nine-month reported ratio was lower than the prior year's, and that fall is the operating story — the central kitchen and head-office base was absorbed as stores were added, lifting operating income to 131 IDR bn [S4]. From FY2026E the model charges the rent itself as an operating cost and removes the right-of-use depreciation from D&A, which adds a wedge equal to the gap between the lease payment and the right-of-use charge: FY2026E opex is therefore 56.0% of sales, not the reported ratio, and it eases to 54.9% by FY2030E as store density rises [S4 p.9]. The consequence is that FY2026E EBITDA of 249.1 is struck after rent, so its 11.1% margin is not comparable with FY2025's filed 19.6%, which is before rent: at FY2025A revenue the same treatment would show the filed EBITDA of 293.3 less the 150 IDR bn of lease payments paid that year. That is the honest economic margin, and it is the one the DCF uses [S2][S4].

Depreciation drives the model, so the decomposition matters. The notes give 88.2 IDR bn of owned fixed-asset depreciation and 105 IDR bn of right-of-use depreciation on store leases for FY2025 [S2 p.41][S2 p.44]. We model the owned charge only, 5.4% of revenue, and charge the lease as rent: keeping right-of-use depreciation in D&A and adding it back while the rent also leaves as cash would credit the same lease twice. The owned assets depreciate over four to eight years and the lease book over three to five, so both grow with the store count [S2][S4]. Hence EBITDA is not comparable with a filer that expenses rent below the line, and the capex that matters is the fit-out rather than the store shell the landlord owns — which is why the replacement anchor for terminal capex is the owned-asset charge of 88.2 IDR bn a year.

Cash generation is where the record has to be read carefully, because the accounting statement flatters it. Operating cash flow was 317 IDR bn in FY2025 against net profit of Rp90.1bn, and 280 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 against 90.0 IDR bn, so the accruals ratio is negative in both periods: accounting profit understates cash [S2][S4]. Part of that is structural, because customers pay at the counter while suppliers are paid on terms. But the largest item is the lease treatment: lease payments of 150 IDR bn in FY2025 and 152 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 sit in financing, so they are not deducted from operating cash flow, and the right-of-use depreciation they correspond to is added back [S2][S4]. Charge the rent where it belongs and the picture inverts: operating cash flow of 317 IDR bn less capex of 192 IDR bn less lease payments of 150 IDR bn leaves nothing in FY2025, and the nine-month equivalent of 280 IDR bn less capex of 191 IDR bn less lease payments of 152 IDR bn is negative before a single new store is opened [S2][S4]. That is why the cash balance fell from Rp327.5bn to 233 IDR bn [S4]. It is not an earnings-quality failure — the cash is real, it is committed to landlords — but the conventional frame of "profitable growth" misses it.

The divergence flags are absent on the lines the screen tests. Trade receivables fell over the nine months while revenue rose by more than half, and inventory grew by about a third against cost of sales up by more than half, so inventory days fell from the high eighties to the low eighties [S4]. Nothing in either line suggests sales being booked that the counter did not take. The line that did move is other current assets, 45.8 IDR bn against a small balance at the 2025 year-end, and it is prepayments and advances tied to the store build rather than a receivable [S4]. There is no capitalised development cost, no related-party receivables of consequence, and no sign of margin expansion accompanied by deteriorating cash conversion; cash conversion improved as the margin improved [S2]. Our earnings-quality verdict is clean: no divergence flag on the working capital, and the funding gap is the lease rather than the ledger.

Capex and working capital both need their derivation, because the capex path was the input the red team challenged as unsourced. The company budgeted 250 IDR bn for 2026 against 100 new outlets, and nine-month additions of 191 IDR bn are running close to that budget [S3][S4]. The 2025 actual was 192 IDR bn, roughly two billion rupiah for each of the roughly ninety net outlets added in the year, which is what a company-operated coffee-shop fit-out costs at this scale [S2]. We start 2026 at 11.2% of revenue — below the 2025 actual of 12.8% because revenue grows by half while the capex budget grows by less than a third — and fade to 8.5% by FY2030E and 7.2% in the terminal year: new-store capex is proportional to the number of stores added, that number shrinks as a percentage of the base, and the terminal ratio has to cover replacement of the owned assets — depreciating at 5.4% of revenue — plus capacity growth at the long-run rate [S2][S3]. Right-of-use depreciation is the landlord's charge, not a capex requirement, because the rent that replaces it is already in operating cost. Holding the FY2026 ratio flat would cut the discounted cash flow substantially; that sensitivity is in the valuation section. Working capital is negative, -4.6% of sales in FY2026E, because stores collect at the counter and pay suppliers on terms; we hold it at the latest actual rather than crediting a release [S4].

The balance sheet is liquid and the debt is now bank debt only. At the end of September the group held 233 IDR bn of cash plus a small restricted balance, against a bank loan of 8.0 IDR bn and lease liabilities of 270 IDR bn [S4]. The model carries the bank loan as debt and charges the lease as rent, so net debt of Rp-294.3bn in FY2026E — negative, because cash exceeds the loan — is the right basis for valuation rather than an artifact: the lease liability is excluded because the rent that services it is already in the cash flow, and including it would deduct the same obligation twice [S4]. Equity is Rp782.5bn on our forecast with no minority interest, and the current ratio is adequate once the lease liability is separated from trade payables [S4]. The one constraint is that accumulated losses remain negative, which is a legal barrier to dividends rather than a solvency issue [S3][S4].

Capital allocation is simple: everything is reinvested. The payout ratio is zero, the company has never paid a dividend, and the annual general meeting confirmed that none can be paid while the retained-earnings account is negative [S3]. The IPO proceeds went into new outlets, the donut subsidiary and working capital, there is no buyback and no bond programme, and the only material financing decision is how fast to add leases [S2][S3]. Because free cash after rent is thin to negative at the current growth rate, reinvestment is funded by the IPO proceeds as well as by operations, which is why the cash balance is falling while the business is profitable [S4]. For a company at this stage that is the right policy; for the minority shareholder it means the return has to come from the value of the estate, not from cash returned along the way, and it means the funding decision is a live risk rather than a balance-sheet detail.

Our forecast reaches Rp4,450.8bn of revenue and Rp519.6bn of EBITDA by FY2030E, with net profit of Rp222.4bn and free cash flow to the firm of Rp98.0bn after the rent charge — the FCFF definition adds back only the owned depreciation and subtracts capex, while the rent is already inside operating cost, so the line is an honest shareholder cash flow rather than one that ignores the landlord [S4]. Return on equity fades from 13.9% toward 10.9% as the equity base built by retained earnings catches up with the returns, which is the arithmetic of a capital-consuming roll-out rather than a deterioration in the business [S2].

We value Fore as a compounder, not a cyclical: the asset is a store programme still being built at the end of any short explicit period, so the value sits in the cash flows after the build and a discounted cash flow is the only method that expresses it. We keep one cross-check, an earnings multiple at 30% of the blend, struck on trailing earnings and therefore penalising a company growing at this rate [S2]. That drops the starter template's third method because of the lease: an enterprise-value multiple compares an EBITDA struck after the rent with peer multiples struck before it, so the two sides are not on the same basis unless computed on EBITDAR, which the peer set does not report. Rather than publish a cross-check we know to be inconsistent, we set it to zero weight and rely on the P/E, which is an equity method — net income already carries the lease because the rent is in operating cost [S2][S4]. The engine flags two methods against a house standard of three; we accept the flag. At the blend the shares are worth Rp166 against a Rp555 price, while the probability-weighted one-year target is Rp286; because the P/E is the lower of the two methods, weighting it more heavily pulls the blend down, not up.

The cost of capital is built in the open, line by line, because the review asked us to reproduce it. It starts from a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4% and an equity risk premium for a mature market of 4.2%; it adds a country risk premium of 2.5% rather than using an emerging-market premium outright, which is the house build; it applies an unlevered beta of 0.85 that we set above the staples default because coffee is a discretionary, ticket-price-led category; it levers that to 0.85 at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.00 on a capital structure that is 99.8% equity and 0.2% debt; and it deducts a sovereign default spread of 1.6% from the risk-free rate before applying the beta, because the rupiah government yield already prices the risk of default that the equity risk premium prices again. The build is therefore (7.4% − 1.6%) + 0.85 × (4.2% + 2.5%) = 11.5% cost of equity. Debt costs 9.45% before tax, so at the 22.0% tax rate used in the WACC shield the after-tax cost is the pre-tax rate scaled by the untaxed share of each rupiah of interest — the pre-tax rate less the tax shield — and it is that product, not the pre-tax figure, that enters the blend, which is why the WACC at 11.5% is below the cost of equity. That 22.0% is the WACC's tax input and not the rate the company pays: the profit-and-loss rate the model runs is 26.0% in FY2026E, easing to 24.0% from FY2029E, and those are the rates inside the FCFF and the earnings, because the shield is discounted at the statutory rate while the forecast carries the rate the filings show being paid [S4]. Two debt rates appear in this report and they are not the same number: the model's finance-cost line runs on the bank borrowing rate of 7.40%, the recorded bank interest over opening bank debt once the lease liability is separated out, because the lease interest is now inside the rent charged in operating cost [S0][S2]; the WACC uses the marginal cost of new borrowing, 9.45%, because the discount rate has to price capital committed today rather than the average of a book built over the last three years. Using the book rate in the WACC would understate it and flatter the value. The rate and premium inputs are the house macro deck's, not the company's: the filings disclose no cost of capital, and the only company-specific input is the beta, set from the consumer-staples distribution and the observed debt-to-equity ratio [S0]. We add no small-float premium although the free float is 21.1%, because float is a liquidity risk handled in the risk section rather than a reason to lift the discount rate off the band [S0].

The base case is a ten-year explicit forecast because the estate is mid-build: a shorter window would capitalise a half-built store count in the terminal year and flatter or penalise the answer depending on the year chosen. The model's free cash flow to the firm is Rp-24.6bn in FY2026E and Rp98.0bn by FY2030E, and both are after the rent: operating cost carries the lease payments on every outlet, and only the owned-asset depreciation is added back, so the landlord is paid inside the cash flow rather than through a separate deduction [S2][S4]. The FY2025A line in the table is the as-filed history and is pre-rent: the gap between model FCFF of 119.5 and operating cash flow of 317 IDR bn less capex of 192 IDR bn less lease payments of 150 IDR bn [S2] is the correction, and it is made once, in the forecast, on the nine-month lease-payment ratio [S4]. The terminal value is 66.0% of the enterprise value, which is high but not unusual for a company whose cash flow arrives after the build; we accept it because the terminal assumptions are disciplined rather than convenient, not because the ratio is comfortable.

The obvious objection is that rent on a store that does not exist yet is a cost of growth and belongs inside the return on the capital spent to open it, not in the discounting of a cash flow that predates it. We tested the alternative and rejected it on two grounds. A pre-rent FCFF credits the model with the whole EBITDA of every new store while leaving out the rent that store pays, and most of the terminal estate is stores that do not exist at the valuation date. And a single fixed bridge deduction cannot be right in three scenarios: the rent owed is a function of the estate each scenario builds, so a bridge sized once overcharges the bear and undercharges the bull. Charging the rent in operating cost makes every scenario pay its own rent, which is why the bear is worth Rp33 rather than the negative value a static deduction produced and the bull Rp743 rather than a rent-free figure [S4].

The unit economics that survive the charge are thin, and the card's test states why: growth is manufactured, not declared, so g = reinvestment rate × ROIIC and both terms have to be shown. In the terminal year the model spends 7.2% of revenue on capex against 5.4% of owned depreciation and takes a small working-capital release, which puts net reinvestment at about a third of after-tax EBIT of Rp338.2bn taxed at 24.0%; the 5.0% terminal growth divided by that reinvestment rate implies an ROIIC in the mid-teens, some three points above the 11.5% WACC. Nearer in it is higher: after-tax EBIT of Rp177.0bn against Rp127.4bn the year before, on reinvestment of capex of Rp305.6bn less D&A of Rp153.4bn plus the working-capital build, is a return of roughly thirty per cent, fading toward the terminal figure as the base matures. Both ends clear the cost of capital, which is why the estate is worth building; what they do not justify is the entry multiple, because the reinvestment is funded at a return in the teens against a multiple the shares carry in the high teens. The base case's post-rent EBITDA margin of 11.7% is already struck after the lease payments, and free cash after rent and capex is a small fraction of that EBITDA in the terminal year [S2][S4].

The multiple-survival test is the discipline on the terminal value, and it has to be struck on the undiscounted number. The terminal value is FY2035E free cash flow of Rp168.4bn grown one year at 5.0% and capitalised at the 11.5% WACC less that growth: against FY2035E EBITDA of Rp646.1bn that is a low single-digit multiple, and against EBIT of Rp338.2bn a high single-digit one. The entry multiple on the same post-rent basis is 18.7x of FY2026E EBITDA — market capitalisation plus the model's forecast net cash; recast on the reported September position, cash of 233 IDR bn less bank debt of 8.0 IDR bn with the lease liability excluded because the rent already appears, it rises by a fraction of a turn, which does not change the comparison [S4][S0]. The exit is under a quarter of the entry, so the DCF assumes the shares de-rate to what a buyer would pay for a mature estate growing at 5.0% — that de-rating, not a cautious operating forecast, is the largest single reason the value sits where it does. The enterprise-value multiple is still not a cross-check, because the peer EBITDA is struck before rent and ours after it; the P/E is, because both sides sit after the lease obligation.

The cross-check points the same way as the cash flow, though it no longer lands as close. The engine strikes the peer multiple on FY2025A earnings, so the P/E returns Rp97 against a peer median of 9.6, -50.2% from the cash-flow value [S0]. The cash-flow value is the higher of the two because it reaches a mature estate in which the operating cost ratio has eased and the store programme has stopped consuming capital, while the trailing multiple is struck on a year in which rent, right-of-use depreciation and the fit-out programme take their share of a smaller store base. For a company that grew revenue by more than half in the following nine months a trailing multiple is not a fair comparison; on forward earnings the shares are 35.4x FY2027E and 28.8x FY2028E, a premium to the mature peer set for two more years of growth. Both answers are below the price.

The sensitivity grid moves the WACC through the band and the terminal growth around our assumption, and it shows what the reader should already suspect: the answer is more sensitive to the discount rate than to any single operating assumption, because so much of the value is terminal. It also shows that the gap to the price cannot be closed with a discount rate: at the bottom of the house band and a point more terminal growth the cash-flow value is still a fraction of the price, and a point higher WACC takes it toward zero. What closes the gap is a different operating path, which is what the scenarios test rather than what the grid can. The operating sensitivities that matter are the two the review pressed: the capex ratio, because holding the FY2026 level rather than fading it materially reduces the discounted cash flow and credits the estate with none of the operating leverage that comes with maturity, and the rent, because every percentage point of revenue charged as rent is a permanent call on operating cash and cuts the cash-flow value by the present value of that rent after tax. That asymmetry is why we do not present the target as a precise number, and why the scenario range is wider than the sensitivity range.

The reverse DCF is the most useful check on the market's view. At Rp555 the price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 39.0% against our 26.0%; the solver adds the gap to the whole growth path, so the market is paying for a store programme that outgrows ours in every forecast year [S2]. The target is a twelve-month number built in two steps: the base case rolled forward at the cost of equity is Rp185, and weighting the bear at Rp33 and the bull at Rp743 with half the weight on the base gives Rp286. The bull quarter is what lifts the target above today's base value, which is precisely why we report the base case on its own: at Rp185 the shares are worth a fraction of the price even if the bull never happens.

The de-rating risk is the strongest argument against the target, and it is already in the blend rather than hidden in a scenario. Indonesian consumer names with premium multiples have spent a decade compressing, and a company trading on 35.4x forward earnings with a 21.1% float and no same-store disclosure is exactly the profile that de-rates when growth slows [S0][S2]. The scenarios shock operating drivers, not multiples, so the de-rating is expressed through the cross-check, worth Rp97 at the peer median and carrying 30% of the blend. On either path — de-rating or holding today's multiple — the shares are worth less than the price today, which is why the rating is SELL on the base case and not a call that depends on the bull.

The difference between a cash-flow value and a multiple value is usually a statement about time.
A multiple capitalises the next year's earnings and assumes the business after that is worth the
same multiple; a cash flow says what the business earns between now and maturity and what is left
at the end. For a company spending heavily to build an estate, the multiple method charges the
spending against today's earnings and credits none of the stores it buys, while the cash flow
charges the spending and credits the stores. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions.

We rank each risk by the likelihood of it biting inside the forecast horizon and the impact on the target if it does, and we size only the ones that change the base case rather than the ones that merely make the quarters noisy.

**Competition and discounting — high likelihood, high impact.** The category is crowded, the company itself describes intense competition and consumers choosing on experience rather than product, and the discount line in the nine-month revenue is already material [S2][S4]. A price war would hit gross margin first and store productivity second, and the company has limited room to respond because it has said it will not raise menu prices this year [S3]. This is the risk that turns the bear case from a slowdown into a margin event.

**Consumer and macro — medium likelihood, high impact.** A small discretionary ticket is sensitive to real incomes, fuel prices and purchasing power, and management has already flagged fuel-cost pressure as a live issue [S3]. If traffic falls, the operating leverage that produced the margin improvement works in reverse: the central kitchen and head office do not shrink with the ticket count, and the depreciation of the estate is fixed [S2].

**Input cost and currency — high likelihood, medium impact.** Green coffee, dairy and packaging are globally priced and dollar-linked, and the price locks that protect the current margin expire [S3]. A weaker rupiah or a coffee-price spike would compress gross margin with a lag, and the company's mitigation — annual contracts rather than menu prices — defers rather than removes the risk [S3].

**Execution and cannibalisation — medium likelihood, high impact.** The estate grew by about two fifths in a single year and another 100 outlets are planned, and the company does not disclose same-store sales, so the market cannot see whether new stores are taking sales from old ones [S2][S3]. Poor site selection would show up as slower revenue per outlet and a rising operating cost ratio, and only after the lease is signed [S2].

**Data protection and cyber — occurred, impact unquantified.** On 28 October and again on 1 November 2026 the company confirmed unauthorised access to one of its customer-data platforms affecting about 5.7 million customer accounts, and reported the incident to the regulator, Komdigi [S5]. The disclosure names no fine, no sanction and no cost, so nothing is charged in our base case; what it establishes is that the customer data the loyalty and app programme runs on is a live regulatory exposure and that a breach lands directly on the brand of a company selling an experience. We treat it as an unquantified risk rather than a modelled cost, because an enforcement fine would be a charge against a profit line that is already thin after rent, and the reputational cost would show up as slower store productivity, which the company does not disclose [S5].

**Regulatory and accounting — low likelihood, medium impact.** There is no product price control and no concession regime; the relevant exposure is lease accounting and disclosure, where a change in the lease standard or in the treatment of the right-of-use asset would move reported EBITDA and net debt without changing cash [S2][S4]. The exchange's free-float rule is satisfied today, but a further concentrated placement would not change the operating story [S0].

**Governance and control — low likelihood, medium impact.** The controlling shareholder holds 78.9% through Fore Holdings, and the public holds the balance, so minority holders depend on the controller's discipline rather than on a balanced board [S2]. We use the company's own register rather than the data pack's insider figure, which is larger and does not reconcile with the float; the annual report states the holding and the remainder in the same sentence, and that is the number a shareholder is entitled to rely on [S2]. Related-party trade payables are small relative to the total, which is the reassuring part, but the structure is a venture holding company with a long horizon and no obligation to return cash [S2].

**Funding and liquidity of the rollout — medium-to-high likelihood, high impact.** This is the risk the lease correction exposes and the previous draft of this report understated. Free cash after rent and capex was negative in FY2025 and again in the first nine months of 2026, when operating cash flow of 280 IDR bn was less than capex of 191 IDR bn plus lease payments of 152 IDR bn, and the gap was met by running cash down from Rp327.5bn to 233 IDR bn [S2][S4]. The company has no material borrowings, the retained-earnings account is negative so no dividend is possible, and the 2026 capex budget of 250 IDR bn plus the leases signed with each new store have to be funded from what is left. If the store programme continues at the guided pace and operating cash does not improve, the funding options are a slower rollout — which cuts the growth the valuation rests on — or new equity into a float of 21.1%, which is the discounted placement outcome in the bear case [S3][S0].

**Liquidity — medium likelihood, medium impact.** The free float is 21.1% and the three-month average daily traded value is IDR3.7bn, which is adequate for a position but not deep [S0]. A sponsor sell-down would improve the float and the index case while putting supply on the tape, and the stock has already traded through a wide range this year [S0].

The scenarios mirror each other, and each carries four shocks on the same drivers. The bear cuts revenue growth by eight points a year, takes a point and a half off gross margin, adds two points to the operating cost ratio and adds two points to capex intensity because a truncated rollout costs more per outlet once scale is lost; the bull does the same four things in reverse [S2]. The fourth pair is the asset-light path: the bull's two-point capex saving is part of the estate converted to franchise or landlord-funded fit-out with the central kitchen supplying more outlets per rupiah, and the bear's addition is that mechanism backwards. Nothing else changes — the discount rate, the tax rate, the lease correction and the terminal growth are the base case's — so the outcome gap is operations, not valuation inputs [S2]. Because the rent sits inside operating cost, each scenario pays the rent its own estate implies, which is why the bear value is positive rather than floored at nil: a smaller estate owes less rent. The probabilities are a quarter each for bear and bull with the base at one half, giving Rp33, Rp185 and Rp743; the asymmetry in outcome is the DCF's convexity, not an asymmetric set of assumptions.

The signposts we would act on are specific. Two consecutive quarters in which revenue per average outlet falls would tell us the new stores are cannibalising the old ones; a gross margin below the FY2025 level for a full year would tell us the price locks have stopped working; lease liabilities growing faster than revenue would tell us the estate is being bought with obligations rather than cash; and any conversion of company-operated stores to a franchise model would change the capital intensity and the quality of the earnings [S2][S4]. On the other side, a same-store sales disclosure, a second consecutive year of operating-margin expansion, or a credible plan to lift the free float would each justify a higher weight on the bull case.

The pre-mortem is short. If this call is wrong on the downside, it will be because rent and capex together consume the cash the stores throw off, the rollout slows or is funded by a discounted placement into a small float, and the multiple de-rates before the operating leverage can be proved. If it is wrong on the upside, the mechanism is most likely the rent charge itself: we applied today's lease-payment ratio to the whole estate in every forecast year, and if that ratio falls as stores mature — revenue per outlet rising against rent that steps only with renewals — the charge is too large and the cash flow is worth more than we say. The second upside mechanism is the asset-light path, in which the capex saving compounds and the rent moves off the balance sheet with it. Both are measurable from the company's disclosures, both are in the signposts above, and neither is in the base case [S2][S4]. The defence of the rating is not that the business is weak; it is that the cash flow after the landlord is paid does not support the price, and the multiple evidence agrees.

Fore is a controlled company and the report should be read with that in mind. Fore Holdings Pte. Ltd. is the controlling shareholder with 78.9%, PT Otten Coffee Indonesia holds a token residual, and the public holds the balance, with the free float at 21.1% [S2][S0]. We use the company's own register rather than the data pack's insider figure, which is larger and which, added to the float, sums to more than the company: the annual report states the controlling holding and the remainder in the same sentence, and that is the version we carry [S2]. Because the controlling holder is a Singapore entity, the register is majority foreign by attribution, which matters for index inclusion and for the kind of shareholder that can be tapped in a placement [S2]. The annual report states that the holding company owns no other entity besides Fore, which is the relevant fact for related-party risk: this is not a conglomerate using a listed vehicle to fund sibling businesses [S2]. The controller's representatives on the board are tied to East Ventures, the venture investor that backed the company before the listing, and the president commissioner is an East Ventures founder [S2].

The board is small and only partly independent. There are six commissioners, of whom two are independent, and four directors led by the president director; the independent share is a minority of the board, which is permitted but leaves minority holders relying on the controller's self-discipline [S2]. The audit committee sits under the commissioners and the annual report describes an internal audit function and a risk-management system, but we did not find an independent director with retail or consumer-operations experience deep enough to challenge the expansion plan on operating grounds [S2]. That is a governance observation rather than a red flag: the board has approved the strategy and the company has delivered the store count it promised.

The audit is clean and the auditor is a mid-tier international network. The FY2025 accounts were audited by Mirawati Sensi Idris, a Moore Global member firm, with an unqualified opinion in all material respects under Indonesian standards [S2]. A mid-tier auditor is normal for a company of this size and is not itself a concern, but it is a reason to read the notes rather than the headline: the lease, revenue-recognition and related-party notes are where a fast-growing retailer has discretion, and we have used the notes rather than the MD&A for the depreciation and lease figures in this report [S2][S4].

Related-party flows are small and we checked them explicitly. Trade payables to related parties are under one per cent of total trade payables and, measured against the group's revenue and its total assets, well under a tenth of one per cent in each case, so the flow test that matters on the house screen comes out clean [S4]. Other related-party payables are a few billion rupiah against a much larger third-party balance, and the related-party long-term loan that existed at the end of 2024 was fully repaid during 2025 [S2]. There are no related-party receivables of consequence and no guarantees to the controlling shareholder's other ventures disclosed [S2]. On the house screen this is the modal Indonesian value-destruction channel, and here it is not present at a scale that matters.

The dividend record is empty by design. The company has never paid a dividend, the payout ratio in our forecast is zero, and the annual general meeting confirmed that no distribution is possible while the retained-earnings account remains negative after the accumulated losses of the build phase [S3][S4]. The IPO proceeds were earmarked for new outlets, the donut subsidiary and working capital, the company has no bonds outstanding, and there has been no rights issue, buyback or share cancellation since listing [S2]. The capital-structure flags on our checklist are therefore absent, with the free float the only structural item: a controlling holder at this level and a float this size mean the stock can be moved by a single seller [S0].

The exchange status is clean and we checked it first, because on IDX the board and notation come before any fundamental screen. The shares are listed on the main board and the annual report confirms that during 2025 there was no temporary trading suspension and no delisting [S2 p.12]. We found no special notation — going concern, negative equity, late filing, or the special-monitoring board — in the filings we hold or in the exchange register we can access, and the free-float requirement is met, so there is no regime flag that would make the name untradeable or class it as manipulation-risk. The screens that would matter here are the lease and the cash burn, not the listing status.

On ESG the disclosures are real but not quantified. The company reports a TJSL programme, an organic-waste initiative in Solo, barista training and participation in the World of Coffee event, and it frames sustainability around coffee culture and community rather than around emissions or packaging targets [S2]. For a business selling in single-use cups with an agricultural supply chain, packaging and coffee sourcing are the material exposures, and neither carries a published target or costed transition plan in the material we reviewed [S2]. We do not treat that as a valuation input today; we do treat it as a disclosure gap a larger institutional base would eventually force closed.

The dated catalysts are the results calendar and the store programme. FY2026 results in February 2027 are the first full-year test of whether the operating-margin improvement held through the fourth quarter and whether capex came in against the company's own budget [S3]. First-quarter 2027 trading follows in April, with the strong nine-month base of 2026 in the comparator, and the annual general meeting and public expose in May typically carry the next store target, the capex budget and any change to the dividend policy [S2][S3]. Before all of those, the year-end store count in December is the cleanest read on whether the planned 100 additions were delivered, and whether the donut format and the central kitchen are producing the food attachment they were built for [S3].

Between updates we watch a short list of operating numbers rather than the share price. Revenue per average outlet is the substitute for same-store sales, which the company does not disclose; gross margin is the read on input costs and pricing; the operating cost ratio is the read on whether the central base is being absorbed; lease liabilities against revenue are the read on how the estate is being financed; and operating cash flow less lease payments is the read on whether the growth is self-funding [S2][S4]. The balance-sheet divergence screen is unchanged from the financial section: inventory days fell as sales outgrew the inventory build, and the jump in other current assets is prepayments tied to the store build rather than a receivable — a timing item we watch, not an earnings-quality flag [S4].
